p: I was born in eighteen eleven, in a village in Shropshire, not far from the Severn gorge at Coalbrookdale, where in seventeen nine Abraham Darby first smelted iron using coke instead of charcoal, and where in seventeen seventy-nine his grandson built the first great bridge of iron in the world, which still stands. As a child I was taken to see the furnaces at night, glowing red along the river, and I thought I had been shown the mouth of hell. I have lived my whole life inside the greatest change in the material condition of mankind since the coming of farming, and I am still not certain whether I was right.

The phrase Industrial Revolution will be made popular, the Encyclopaedia tells me, by a young Oxford historian named Arnold Toynbee in lectures a few years hence, though French writers used it earlier. It describes the transformation, beginning in Britain in the second half of the eighteenth century, from an economy of farms, workshops and hand labour to one of factories, machines and mineral power. For all of previous history, the energy available to mankind came from the muscles of men and animals, from wind and running water, and from burning wood. In the Industrial Revolution, men learned to harness the energy stored in coal, through the steam engine, and the result was an increase in the production of goods that has continued, I am told, to the present day of the Encyclopaedia, and spread across the whole world.

Historians have argued endlessly why this happened first in Britain, and the Encyclopaedia lists many reasons. Britain had abundant coal and iron, often close together and close to water. It had a large and growing market at home and in its colonies, and a great overseas trade. Its agriculture had become productive enough to feed a growing population that no longer worked the land. It had secure property, a stable government, a sound system of banking, canals and roads, and patent laws that rewarded inventors. Wages in Britain were high and coal cheap, so that it paid to replace labour with machines driven by coal. And it had a culture of practical tinkering, of artisans and gentlemen who met in societies such as the Lunar Society of Birmingham, so named because they met at the full moon, so as to have light to ride home by, to talk of chemistry, engines and pottery.

The revolution began in cotton. Spinning thread and weaving cloth had been done by hand, by families in their cottages, for thousands of years. In a few decades, a series of inventions changed it entirely: John Kay's flying shuttle in seventeen thirty-three, which doubled the speed of weaving; James Hargreaves's spinning jenny, about seventeen sixty-four, which allowed one worker to spin eight threads at once; Richard Arkwright's water frame, driven by a water wheel, for which he built at Cromford in Derbyshire in seventeen seventy-one what may be called the first modern factory; and Samuel Crompton's mule, which spun fine thread in enormous quantities. Raw cotton came from the slave plantations of the American South, and the cheap cloth of Lancashire went out to clothe the world, ruining, among others, the ancient hand-weavers of India.

The steam engine was the heart of it. Thomas Newcomen, a Devon ironmonger, built in seventeen twelve the first practical engine, a huge and wasteful machine that used the pressure of the atmosphere, acting on a piston when steam beneath it was condensed, to pump water out of mines. James Watt, an instrument maker at the University of Glasgow, repairing a model of Newcomen's engine in seventeen sixty-five, saw that it wasted most of its fuel by heating and cooling the cylinder at every stroke, and invented a separate condenser, which made it several times more efficient. In partnership with the Birmingham manufacturer Matthew Boulton, who told James Boswell, Dr Johnson's biographer, when he visited the works, I sell here, sir, what all the world desires to have: power, he made engines that could turn the wheels of factories, anywhere, without the need of a river.

Then came the locomotive. Richard Trevithick ran a steam carriage on rails in Wales in eighteen hundred and four. George Stephenson's Rocket won the trials for the Liverpool and Manchester Railway in eighteen twenty-nine, at a speed of nearly thirty miles an hour, and the railway, opened the following year, was the first to carry passengers and goods on a timetable, wholly by steam. At its opening, William Huskisson, a former government minister, stepped into the path of the Rocket and was killed, the first famous victim of the railway age. Within twenty years Britain was covered with railways, and the journey from London to Edinburgh, which took a fortnight in my grandfather's youth, takes, today, about ten hours.

The human cost was very great. The new factory towns, Manchester, Leeds, Birmingham, grew so fast that they had no proper drainage, water or housing, and the workers lived in cellars and courts of horrible squalor, where cholera and typhus raged and half the children died before the age of five. Men, women and young children worked twelve, fourteen and more hours a day in the mills, under a discipline of bells and fines that no peasant had ever known. Mr Engels, a German manufacturer's son in Manchester, described it in a book of eighteen forty-five, and his friend Karl Marx built upon such observations a theory of history which I do not share, but which the Encyclopaedia tells me will move a large part of mankind in the next century. Mr Dickens described it in Hard Times. Mr Blake, the poet, called the mills dark and satanic.

Yet the Encyclopaedia also records the other side, which my own generation could only hope for. Over the following century, real wages rose, Parliament passed laws limiting the hours of women and children, the towns acquired sewers and clean water, and the immense increase in the production of goods slowly raised the condition of the mass of the people above anything known before. For the first time in history, the Encyclopaedia says, the total wealth of a society grew year after year, steadily, faster than its population, so that each generation could expect to be richer than the last. That has never happened before in the history of mankind. It has made possible everything in the rest of these lectures, for good and for ill. And it is founded, I am told, upon the burning of coal and its successors in such quantities that the very air of the planet has been altered. The furnaces of Coalbrookdale were, perhaps, a mouth of hell after all. But it was a hell that fed and clothed the world.
